newsitem.title: INDIA: India reforms reducing bad loans - RBI governor.
newsitem.headline: India reforms reducing bad loans - RBI governor.

text.p: India's state banks are rapidly improving their loan-recovery rate as a result of financial reforms made four years ago, Reserve Bank of India (RBI) Governor C. Rangarajan said on Friday.

His comments came the same day that Finance Minister P. Chidambaran told parliament that he had ordered an investigation into The Indian Bank, following its 13.36 billion rupees ($374 million) loss in 1995-96 (April-March). The bank had a large number of non-performing loans in its portfolio.

"I expect that in the next year or two we shall bring down the level of non-performing assets as a proportion of total assets to 10 per cent," the central bank governor told a banking and investment conference here.
State-owned banks were now making more efforts to recover such loans rather than taking the easy, if costly, option of writing them off, he said.

Chidambaram's announcement of the probe sparked accusations in the Lok Sabha (Lower House) that top industrial and business houses had been let off the hook while small borrowers were being chased, the Press Trust of India (PTI) reported.
The Indian Bank reported the losses in July, but has not issued any statements to explain them.
Rangarajan said loan recovery accounted for more than half of last year's reduction in banks' non-performing assets.
"Recovery is an important thing and I can tell you this is the route banks are now taking," Rangarajan said.
The central bank governor said that non-performing assets currently stood at around 19 percent, but after taking account of provisions against bad loans the net figure would be substantially lower.
Also, a central bank request that banks report the performance of loans made after the introduction of bank reforms in 1992-93 showed a dramatic reduction in the number going bad.
"The non-performing assets are in the region of three percent, which is an internationally acceptable standard," Rangarajan told a Euromoney Publications conference.

The banking reforms were also showing results in other ways, he said. Aside from making the banks adopt more prudent procedures, the reforms also aimed to remove external constraints on their profitability and make them more competitive.
Rangarajan said that as a group, public sector banks had turned the corner in 1994-95 (April-March) and the net loss they recorded last year had to be interpreted carefully.

The loss recorded last year stemmed from provisions against non-performing assets and for depreciation on government securities, he said. The provision for the depreciation on government securities amounted to 24.3 billion rupees and was regarded as an "internal reserve", not a loss or cash outflow from banks.
A moderation in interest rates on government securities gave Rangarajan some grounds for expecting an improvement in profits in 1996-97.
He said the net loss of 3.73 billion rupees that the 27 public sector banks showed in the last financial year (1995/96) followed a net profit of 11.16 billion rupees in 1994/95.
